To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) there is no end-to-end verifiability system that is secure against a malicious voting authority and (2) there is no privacy-preserving end-to-end verificability system that is not vulnerable to coercion of voters.
the attacks we have considered can be classified into three groups: attacks on the integrity, attacks on the coercion resistance, and attacks on the privacy.

(i) all voting systems are vulnerable to some kind of attack; (ii) there is no voting system which is simultaneously secure and verifiable; (iii) all voting systems can be attacked in some way, even if the attack requires the collusion of a very large number of voters or election administrators.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: What are the theoretical limits on the security of end-to-end verifable voting systems? What are the security tradeoffs that need to be considered when designing such a system?
the question: What are known vulnerabilities and weaknesses of end-to-end verified voting systems, and what are their consequences?
the security of e-voting systems and their ability to withstand attacks by an active, malicious adversary.

there are no secure voting systems.
no existing system is secure against all possible attacks.
there is no end-to-end voting system that can withstand all possible attacks.
